involve in.transitivity: **transitive** in both — *involve her in the planning*; and the entail sense takes an object or a bare gerund with no preposition: *the job involves traveling*, ✗ *the job involves to travel*.
involve in.passive: **yes** in the participation sense, where the passive is the usual form — *she was involved in the campaign*, *he got involved with the union*. The entail sense resists a *by*-phrase: ✗ *a lot of travel is involved by the job*.

keep up with, catch up with, catch up on.verb type: action — dynamic; all three are durative and take the progressive: *she's catching up on three weeks of email*, *he isn't keeping up with the rent*.
keep up with, catch up with, catch up on.transitivity: **intransitive** — phrasal-prepositional, so the verb has no direct object and nothing may be inserted: ✗ *keep the news up with*, ✗ *catch my email up on*.
keep up with, catch up with, catch up on.passive: **restricted** — three-word units passivize badly. *The payments couldn't be kept up with* is possible and clumsy; ✗ *the backlog has been caught up on* is not idiomatic. Keep the active.

laugh at.verb type: action — dynamic; a reaction you perform, freely progressive: *they were laughing at him*.
laugh at.transitivity: **intransitive** — the thing amusing you always needs the preposition: ✗ *laugh the joke*. Bare *laugh* stands alone (*everybody laughed*).
laugh at.passive: **yes** — the prepositional passive is fully idiomatic: *he was laughed at by the whole room*, *her projections were laughed at*.

learn about, learn from.verb type: action — dynamic; a process, not a state, and it takes the progressive: *she's learning about soil chemistry*. The past is *learned* in American English.
learn about, learn from.transitivity: **both** — **intransitive** with *about* and *from*; **transitive** bare (*learn the routine*), plus a to-infinitive (*learn to swim*) and a that-clause (*learned that the office had moved*).
learn about, learn from.passive: **restricted** — the bare transitive passivizes (*the routine has to be learned by Friday*, *lessons were learned*), the prepositional frames do not: ✗ *the war was learned about*, ✗ *his father was learned from*.

listen to.verb type: action — dynamic and deliberate, unlike the passive faculty *hear*: *I listened to the whole thing* against *I heard the alarm*.
listen to.transitivity: **intransitive** — the object always needs *to*: ✗ *listen music*, ✗ *listen me*. Bare *listen* stands alone as a command (*Listen.*).
listen to.passive: **restricted** — natural with a person as object (*the engineer wasn't listened to*, *nobody was listened to*), stiff with a thing: ✗ *the album was listened to twice*.

live up to.verb type: action — dynamic; meeting a standard over time, and progressive: *the sequel isn't living up to the hype*.
live up to.transitivity: **intransitive** — phrasal-prepositional, no direct object, and nothing may be inserted: ✗ *live it up to*, which is a different idiom entirely.
live up to.passive: **restricted** — *a promise that was never lived up to* is possible in writing but heavy; American speech keeps the active: *he never lived up to it*.

long for.verb type: **stative** — a sustained emotional state rather than an act, though unlike most statives it takes the progressive freely in literary use: *she was longing for home*.
long for.transitivity: **intransitive** — everything comes through *for*; to put an action after it, drop the preposition and use the infinitive: *long to go home*.
long for.passive: **no** — the verb is intransitive and the prepositional passive is not English: ✗ *home was longed for by the whole crew*. Only the attributive participle survives: *the longed-for reunion*.

look at, look for, look after, look into.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses — reading, hunting, tending, investigating. Bare *look* also has a **linking** use taking an adjective: *look tired*, ✗ *look tiredly*.
look at, look for, look after, look into.transitivity: **intransitive** — every one of the four requires its preposition; the verb takes no bare object: ✗ *look the report*.
look at, look for, look after, look into.passive: **yes** — this family gives English its textbook prepositional passives: *the complaint is being looked into*, *the kids were well looked after*, *the file was never looked at*.

look forward to.verb type: **stative** — an attitude of anticipation, not an act; it is unusual among statives in taking the progressive freely, and both forms are standard: *I look forward to hearing from you*, *I'm looking forward to it*.
look forward to.transitivity: **intransitive** — no direct object; *to* is a **preposition**, so a verb after it must be *-ing*: ✗ *look forward to hear from you*.
look forward to.passive: **restricted** — grammatically available and almost never used; *your reply is looked forward to* is dead commercialese, and ✗ *the meeting is looked forward to by everyone* is not written.

look up to, look down on.verb type: **stative** — standing attitudes of admiration and contempt, not events; the progressive is odd: ✗ *she is looking up to her brother these days*.
look up to, look down on.transitivity: **intransitive** — both are fixed three-word units taking a person through the preposition, and neither can be split: ✗ *look him up to*, ✗ *look down them on*.
look up to, look down on.passive: **yes** — unusually free for prepositional verbs, as the entry notes: *he was looked up to by everyone in the shop*, *she was looked down on for years*.

major in, minor in.verb type: action — dynamic and durative; a course of study you pursue: *she's majoring in biology*.
major in, minor in.transitivity: **intransitive** — the field always comes through *in*, and the verb has no other object: ✗ *she majored biology*, ✗ *she majored to biology*.
major in, minor in.passive: **no** — intransitive, and the prepositional passive does not exist: ✗ *biology was majored in by half her class*.

militate against.verb type: **stative** — a fact or consideration counts as a reason against something; nothing is done, and the subject is never a person: ✗ *the senator militates against the bill*. Not the transitive *mitigate*: ✗ *mitigate against*.
militate against.transitivity: **intransitive** — the conclusion opposed always comes through *against*; there is no bare object: ✗ *militates the conclusion*.
militate against.passive: **no** — intransitive and stative; ✗ *raising rates was militated against*. (Transitive *mitigate*, the word people mean by mistake, passivizes fine: *the damage was mitigated*.)

move for.verb type: action — dynamic and performative: saying it does it, in court or under *Robert's Rules*. Non-progressive in use — *defendant moves for summary judgment*.
move for.transitivity: **intransitive** in this frame — the relief comes through *for*; the verb's other two frames take a to-infinitive (*moved to dismiss*) or a subjunctive clause (*moved that the meeting be adjourned*), never a bare object: ✗ *moved summary judgment*.
move for.passive: **no** — ✗ *summary judgment was moved for* is not idiomatic; the record instead passivizes the ruling: *the motion was granted*, *summary judgment was denied*.

object to.verb type: action — dynamic; a speech act in the courtroom or the meeting (*counsel objected*), and by extension a standing position (*she objects to being called ma'am*).
object to.transitivity: **intransitive** — no direct object, unlike transitive *oppose*: *oppose the merger*, ✗ *oppose to the merger*, against *object to the merger*. Before a clause the preposition drops: *objected that the sample was too small*.
object to.passive: **restricted** — fine in formal minutes and briefs (*the proposal was objected to by two members*, *the exhibit was objected to*), unnatural in speech.

occur to.verb type: action — dynamic but punctual, an idea arriving; it still rejects the progressive: ✗ *it is occurring to me that she was right*. Note the spellings *occurred*, *occurring*.
occur to.transitivity: **intransitive** — the subject is the idea (usually dummy *it* plus a that-clause or infinitive) and *to* takes the person: *it never occurred to him to ask*.
occur to.passive: **no** — intransitive, and the person cannot become a subject: ✗ *I was occurred to*, ✗ *he was never occurred to*.

offset against, set off against.verb type: action — dynamic; an arithmetical operation performed on two quantities of the same kind.
offset against, set off against.transitivity: **transitive** — the amount applied is the direct object and *against* names what it is applied to: *offset the loss against this year's gains*; the object is obligatory: ✗ *offset against the gains*.
offset against, set off against.passive: **yes** — *the loss can be offset against next year's gains*, and the counterweight frame is passive by nature: *the raise was offset by the new premium*.

participate in.verb type: action — dynamic; doing the exercises, not merely being present — compare transitive *attend*, which claims only presence.
participate in.transitivity: **intransitive** — the verb cannot take a bare object: ✗ *participate the study*. Everything comes through *in*.
participate in.passive: **no** — intransitive, and the prepositional passive is unidiomatic: ✗ *the study was participated in by forty volunteers*. Say *forty volunteers took part*.

petition for.verb type: action — dynamic and formal: a filing or a signed request, a single act.
petition for.transitivity: **both** — **intransitive** with *for* alone (*petitioned for review*), **transitive** when the body petitioned is named, which takes no preposition: *petition the board for a hearing*, ✗ *petition to the mayor*.
petition for.passive: **restricted** — the person-object promotes (*the board was petitioned for a hearing*), the *for*-object does not: ✗ *review was petitioned for*.

plan on.verb type: action — dynamic; forming an intention, freely progressive and slightly provisional: *I'm planning on retiring in June*.
plan on.transitivity: **both** — **intransitive** with *on* plus a gerund or noun (*plan on staying*, *plan on rain*); **transitive** bare (*plan the trip*), and with a to-infinitive and no preposition (*plan to stay*).
plan on.passive: **restricted** — the bare transitive passivizes (*the route was planned by a committee*), the prepositional frame does not: ✗ *staying an extra night was planned on*.

point at, point to.verb type: **both** — dynamic in the gesture sense (*she was pointing at the map*); **stative** in the evidential sense, which resists the progressive: ✗ *the data are pointing to a slowdown* is far weaker than *the data point to a slowdown*.
point at, point to.transitivity: **intransitive** in both — ✗ *point the map*. The verb is transitive only when what you aim is the object: *point a finger at him*, *point the camera at the door*.
point at, point to.passive: **restricted** — the gesture sense passivizes with a person (*nobody likes being pointed at*); the evidential sense does not: ✗ *a slowdown is pointed to by the data*.

prefer to.verb type: **stative** — a standing preference, not an act, and it rejects the progressive: ✗ *I am preferring tea to coffee*.
prefer to.transitivity: **transitive** — *prefer tea to coffee*, *prefer walking to driving*; both sides of the comparison must match, so ✗ *prefer to walk to drive* collapses. The object is obligatory: ✗ *she prefers to coffee*.
prefer to.passive: **restricted** — the agentless passive is standard in impersonal writing (*the metric version is preferred to the older one*), but the stative verb refuses a *by*-phrase: ✗ *tea is preferred to coffee by her*.

prepare for.verb type: action — dynamic and durative: *they've been preparing for a strike all month*.
prepare for.transitivity: **both** — **intransitive** with *for* (*prepare for a strike*) or a bare to-infinitive (*prepared to negotiate*); **transitive** with no preposition (*prepare a meal*, *prepare a brief*).
prepare for.passive: **yes** in the transitive frame — *the brief was prepared overnight*. The prepositional frame is **restricted**: *everything had been prepared for* is possible, ✗ *a strike was prepared for by management* is not.

preside over.verb type: action — dynamic and durative; holding the chair while something runs its course, and progressive: *Judge Ellis is presiding over the trial*.
preside over.transitivity: **intransitive** — the verb needs its preposition: ✗ *preside the meeting*, unlike transitive *chair*, *run*, and *oversee*.
preside over.passive: **yes** — one of the fully natural prepositional passives: *the trial was presided over by Judge Ellis*, *a hearing presided over by the deputy commissioner*.

prevail over.verb type: **both** — dynamic in the defeat sense, an achievement (*the plaintiff prevailed over three co-defendants*); **stative** in the be-widespread sense, which rejects the progressive: ✗ *the practice is prevailing in rural counties*, *the prevailing view*.
prevail over.transitivity: **intransitive** in every sense — the opponent comes through *over*, the person you talk around through *on* plus a to-infinitive (*prevailed on her to stay*); ✗ *prevailed the defendant*.
prevail over.passive: **no** for *prevail over* — intransitive: ✗ *the defendant was prevailed over*. But *prevail on* passivizes and is idiomatic: *she was prevailed upon to stay another year*.

prevent from.verb type: action — dynamic; stopping something before it happens.
prevent from.transitivity: **transitive** — the person or thing stopped is the direct object and *from* takes a **gerund**: *prevent him from leaving*, ✗ *prevent him to leave*. Bare transitive is also fine: *prevent an accident*.
prevent from.passive: **yes** — *he was prevented from boarding*, *the leak was prevented*. The passive keeps the same *from* plus *-ing*: ✗ *he was prevented to board*.

protect from, protect against.verb type: action — dynamic and often durative: *the coating is protecting the deck from UV*.
protect from, protect against.transitivity: **transitive** — the person or thing protected is the direct object; the object is obligatory, reflexive if need be: ✗ *protect from the sun* with nobody named. Both prepositions take the same complements.
protect from, protect against.passive: **yes**, and the passive is the everyday form — *the portfolio is protected against inflation*, *she was protected from the worst of it*, *vaccinated against measles*.

provide with, provide for.verb type: **both** — dynamic in the supply and support senses (*the district is providing students with laptops*, *he provided for four children*); **stative** in the drafting sense, which rejects the progressive: ✗ *the lease is providing for a five percent escalator*.
provide with, provide for.transitivity: **both** — **transitive** in *provide students with laptops* and *provide meals*; **intransitive** with the preposition in *provide for a family* and *the contract provides for arbitration*. Not ditransitive in careful writing: ✗ *provide the crew meals*.
provide with, provide for.passive: **yes** — *students were provided with laptops*, *meals were provided for the crew*, and the drafting sense gives a clean prepositional passive: *arbitration is provided for in section 12*.

punish for.verb type: action — dynamic; imposing a penalty, a single act.
punish for.transitivity: **transitive** — the person punished is the direct object, the offense takes *for*, and the penalty takes *by* or *with*: ✗ *punish to him*, ✗ *punish someone of the leak*.
punish for.passive: **yes**, and it is the commoner form — *he was punished for the leak*, *the offense is punishable by five years*.

qualify for.verb type: **both** — **stative** in the eligibility sense, which resists the progressive: ✗ *she is qualifying for the subsidy*; dynamic in the athletic sense (*he qualified for the finals*) and in the transitive hedge sense (*he qualified the claim in a footnote*).
qualify for.transitivity: **both** — **intransitive** with *for* and *as* (*qualifies as a hardship*) and with a bare to-infinitive (*qualified to practice in three states*); **transitive** in the hedge sense: *qualify the statement*.
qualify for.passive: **no** in the stative eligibility sense — ✗ *the subsidy is qualified for by most applicants*. **Yes** in the hedge sense: *the claim was carefully qualified in a footnote*.

react to.verb type: action — dynamic and involuntary, more immediate than considered *respond to*; freely progressive: *the market is reacting to the announcement*.
react to.transitivity: **intransitive** — the stimulus always needs a preposition: ✗ *react the news*. *to* for a stimulus, *with* for chemistry, *against* for a generation pushing back.
react to.passive: **no** — intransitive, and the prepositional passive is not English here: ✗ *the announcement was reacted to badly*. Say *the announcement went over badly*.

reconcile with.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: repairing a relationship, squaring two sets of figures, or coming to accept something (*she's slowly reconciling herself to it*).
reconcile with.transitivity: **both** — **transitive** in *reconcile the statement with the ledger* and in the reflexive *reconcile oneself to*; **intransitive** in *the couple reconciled* and *she reconciled with her father*.
reconcile with.passive: **yes** in the transitive frame — *the two accounts can't be reconciled with each other*, *the figures were reconciled to the ledger*. No passive of the intransitive: ✗ *her father was reconciled with*.

recover from.verb type: action — dynamic; a process in the intransitive sense (*she's still recovering from the surgery*) and a single act of retrieval in the transitive one.
recover from.transitivity: **both** — **intransitive** with *from* naming the illness or setback (*recover from the loss*); **transitive** with no preposition in the get-something-back sense (*recover the data*, *recover damages*), where *from* names the source instead.
recover from.passive: **yes** in the transitive sense — *the stolen equipment was recovered*, *the fees were recovered from the insurer*. **No** in the intransitive: ✗ *the surgery was recovered from*.

recuse from.verb type: action — dynamic and performative: the judge's stepping aside is done by saying so.
recuse from.transitivity: **transitive with a reflexive object** in careful writing — *recuse himself from the case*; American journalism now also runs it **intransitively** (*the judge recused from the case*, *the justice recused*), but a brief keeps *himself*.
recuse from.passive: **no** in edited legal prose — a reflexive object gives nothing to promote: ✗ *he was recused from the case*, which the press nonetheless prints. Use *was disqualified* when you need a passive.

refer to.verb type: **both** — dynamic in the mention, consult, and send-onward senses (*she's referring to the appendix*, *her doctor referred her to a cardiologist*); **stative** in the denote sense, which rejects the progressive: ✗ *'quorum' is referring to the minimum number*.
refer to.transitivity: **both** — **intransitive** with *to* in the mention, consult, and denote senses; **transitive** in the send-onward frame: *refer the patient to a specialist*.
refer to.passive: **yes** — *the case was referred to the appeals panel*, and the prepositional passive is a fixed naming formula: *the area referred to as the Loop*. The denote sense stays awkward with a *by*-phrase: ✗ *the minimum number is referred to by 'quorum'*.

refrain from.verb type: action — dynamic; a deliberate, usually temporary holding back, more occasional than policy-like *abstain from*.
refrain from.transitivity: **intransitive** — the one who refrains is always the subject and the verb never takes an object of its own: ✗ *refrain him from talking* — that verb is *prevent from* or *keep from*.
refrain from.passive: **no** — intransitive, and the prepositional passive is not used: ✗ *comment was refrained from by the office*. Say *the office declined to comment*.

relate to.verb type: **both** — **stative** in the concern sense (*this relates to the second complaint*) and the identify-with sense (*I can relate to her*), both odd in the progressive; dynamic in the narrate sense: *he related the story to us*.
relate to.transitivity: **both** — **intransitive** with *to* in the concern and identify senses; **transitive** in *relate the story to us* and in *relate X to Y*. Kinship needs the participle: *she's related to the governor*, ✗ *she relates to the governor*.
relate to.passive: **restricted** — the narrate sense passivizes (*the story was related to us by her brother*) and the kinship participle is fixed (*she's related to the governor*), but the stative concern sense does not: ✗ *the complaint is related to by this clause*.

relieve of.verb type: action — dynamic; taking a burden or a post away from somebody. Do not confuse it with the adjective of feeling in *relieved at the news*.
relieve of.transitivity: **transitive** — the person always sits between verb and preposition: *relieve someone of something*; the object is obligatory: ✗ *relieve of the reporting requirement*.
relieve of.passive: **yes**, and the passive is far commoner than the active — *he was relieved of his duties*, *she was relieved of having to file the report*.

rely on.verb type: **stative** — a standing state of dependence rather than an act, though it takes the progressive for a temporary arrangement: *we're relying on you this week*.
rely on.transitivity: **intransitive** — the verb never appears without its preposition: ✗ *you can rely me*. A to-infinitive is possible after a person: *rely on her to check it*.
rely on.passive: **restricted** — the prepositional passive is standard in legal and academic prose (*the affidavit was relied on by the court*, *the cases relied upon*), stiff in speech: ✗ *I'm relied on by everybody*.

remind of, remind about.verb type: **both** — dynamic in the prompting sense (*remind me about the deposit*, *remind me to call*); **stative** in the resemblance sense, where nothing happens: *you remind me of my father*.
remind of, remind about.transitivity: **transitive** — the person reminded is always a direct object: ✗ *remind to me*. The verb also takes a to-infinitive after the person (*remind me to call*) and a that-clause (*remind him that it's Tuesday*), neither with a preposition.
remind of, remind about.passive: **yes** in the prompting sense — *staff were reminded of the deadline*, *she was reminded to sign both copies*. The stative resemblance sense resists: ✗ *my father is reminded of by you*.

rescue from.verb type: action — dynamic; a single act of pulling someone out of danger.
rescue from.transitivity: **transitive** — the person or thing rescued is the direct object and *from* names the danger: ✗ *rescue to someone*, ✗ *rescue from the fire* with nobody named.
rescue from.passive: **yes**, and it is the usual news form — *the crew was rescued from the water by a Coast Guard helicopter*, *she was rescued from having to speak*.

reside in.verb type: **stative** — where a person lives or where a power belongs by design; it rejects the progressive: ✗ *sovereignty is residing in the people*, ✗ *the difficulty is residing in the wording*.
reside in.transitivity: **intransitive** — the place, body, or abstraction always comes through *in* (or *at* for a street address, *with* for authority): ✗ *she resides the county*.
reside in.passive: **no** — intransitive and stative, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ *the county is resided in by 40,000 people*, ✗ *the wording is resided in*.

resort to.verb type: action — dynamic; falling back on something you would rather not have used, which is why *resort to force* works and ✗ *resorted to a sensible compromise* sounds odd.
resort to.transitivity: **intransitive** — the verb has no other frame at all: ✗ *he resorted the lie*. *to* is a **preposition**, so a verb after it is *-ing*: *resorted to lying*, ✗ *resorted to lie*.
resort to.passive: **restricted** — available in formal and legal prose (*force was resorted to only after negotiations failed*), unnatural in speech: ✗ *lying was resorted to by him*.

respond to.verb type: action — dynamic, and more considered than involuntary *react to*: *she's responding to every comment herself*. The medical sense is dynamic too: *the tumor responded to radiation*.
respond to.transitivity: **intransitive** — the verb requires its preposition, unlike transitive *answer*: *answer the question* but *respond **to** the question*. A clause attaches to bare *respond*: *he responded that the file was closed*.
respond to.passive: **restricted** — *the letter was never responded to* occurs and is clumsy; the natural passive belongs to the transitive twin, *the letter was never answered*.

rest on.verb type: **stative** — static support, not an event; it rejects the progressive: ✗ *the whole case is resting on proving intent*. The subject is the thing held up, never an agent.
rest on.transitivity: **intransitive** — the support always comes through the preposition: ✗ *the case rests proving intent*. Bare *rest* in court (*the state rests*) is a fixed idiom with no complement.
rest on.passive: **no** — intransitive and stative: ✗ *proving intent is rested on by the whole case*. Compare *rest with*, equally passive-proof: ✗ *the dean is rested with*.

rest with.verb type: **stative** — a standing relation of authority, not an act; it resists the progressive (✗ *the decision is resting with the board*) and has no imperative (✗ *rest with the dean!*).
rest with.transitivity: **intransitive** — the subject is the decision and the *with*-phrase is obligatory: ✗ *final approval rests* is incomplete. There is no direct object: ✗ *rest the board the decision*.
rest with.passive: **no** — intransitive and stative both block it: ✗ *the board is rested with the decision*, ✗ *she is rested with the choice*. Use the active, or switch to *be vested in* / *be up to*.

result in, result from.verb type: **stative-relational** rather than dynamic — it asserts a causal link, so it reads as a generic truth (*higher rates result in fewer refinancings*) and takes the progressive only grudgingly (?*the cuts are resulting in delays*).
result in, result from.transitivity: **intransitive** in both directions; the preposition is obligatory and there is no object: ✗ *result a delay*, ✗ *the storm resulted three outages*.
result in, result from.passive: **no** — nothing to promote: ✗ *four policy changes were resulted in by the audit*, ✗ *the storm was resulted from*. The inverse is built by swapping prepositions, not by the passive: *the delays resulted from a misfiled permit*.

retire from.verb type: **action** — dynamic, a one-time change of status (*he retired from the fire department in March*); *be retired* is the resulting state, an adjective rather than a tense.
retire from.transitivity: **both** — intransitive in the career senses (*she retired*, *retired from the board*, *retired to Tucson*), transitive in the sports and finance senses (*retire his number*, *retire the debt*, *retire a fleet*).
retire from.passive: **restricted** — natural in the transitive senses: *his number was retired the following spring*, *the bonds were retired early*. No passive of the career sense: ✗ *the fire department was retired from*.

rob of.verb type: **action** — dynamic and telic, an event with a victim; the figurative use (*an injury robbed him of a season*) is equally dynamic.
rob of.transitivity: **transitive**, and the object is the victim or the place, not the loot: *rob the bank*, ✗ *rob the money*. The object is obligatory (✗ *two men robbed at closing time*); the *of*-phrase is optional (*they robbed the till*).
rob of.passive: **yes**, and it is the commoner form in the figurative sense — *she was robbed of a promotion by a reorganization*, *the branch was robbed at closing time*.

root for.verb type: **action** — dynamic and atelic, an ongoing attitude expressed as activity; the progressive is the default form (*we're all rooting for you*).
root for.transitivity: **intransitive** — *for* is obligatory before the team or person (✗ *root the underdog*), and any infinitive is licensed by that noun, not by the verb: *rooting for the underdog to win*.
root for.passive: **no** — the prepositional passive does not take here: ✗ *the visiting team was rooted for by half the bar*, ✗ *you're being rooted for*. Use *support* or *back*, which are transitive and passivize freely.

save from.verb type: **action** — dynamic and telic; the rescue is an event with a result (*her seatbelt saved her from far worse*).
save from.transitivity: **both** — transitive with the thing saved as object, and **ditransitive** in the preposition-free frame Americans reach for most: *that saved me an hour*, *it'll save you a trip*.
save from.passive: **yes** — *she was saved from far worse by her seatbelt*, *the cat was saved from the storm drain*. The double-object frame passivizes on the person: *I was saved a trip*.

search for.verb type: **action** — dynamic and atelic in the *for* frame (an activity that may fail), dynamic and telic in the transitive one (*customs searched every bag*).
search for.transitivity: **both** — intransitive with *for* naming what is missing (*searched for her along the river*), transitive with the place or person examined (*search the house*, *search him*), and the two can combine: *searched the property for the equipment*.
search for.passive: **restricted** — excellent in the transitive frame: *every bag on the flight was searched*, *the property was searched for the missing equipment*. No passive of the *for* frame: ✗ *she was searched for for three days* (say *the search for her lasted three days*).

sentence to.verb type: **action** — dynamic and telic, a performative act of the court, complete the moment it is uttered.
sentence to.transitivity: **transitive** — the person sentenced is the direct object and is obligatory (✗ *the judge sentenced to probation*); the *to*-phrase naming the punishment is nearly obligatory too.
sentence to.passive: **yes**, and the passive is the default in news and legal prose: *he was sentenced to eighteen months in federal prison*, *three defendants were sentenced to time served*.

separate from.verb type: **action** — dynamic in the physical senses (*separate the yolks from the whites*); in the descriptive use (*what separates this camera from the cheaper one is the sensor*) it is a **stative** relation, which is why the progressive sounds odd there.
separate from.transitivity: **both** — transitive with an object plus *from* or *into* (*separate the invoices into paid and unpaid*), intransitive with no complement at all (*they separated in April*).
separate from.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *he was separated from his unit for two days*, *the playground is separated from the lot by a chain-link fence*. No passive of the intransitive: ✗ *they were separated in April* means something else.

share with.verb type: **both** — **action** when something is handed over (*she shared her notes with anyone who asked*), **stative** when something is held in common (*he shares a birthday with his grandfather*, *the two houses share a driveway*), where the progressive is odd.
share with.transitivity: **both** — transitive with the thing shared as object and *with* naming the recipient; intransitive with *in* for taking a portion (*junior partners share in the profits*), where no object is possible.
share with.passive: **restricted** — fine in the transitive giving sense: *the notes were shared with the whole team*. No passive of *share in* (✗ *the profits were shared in*) and none of the stative sense (✗ *a driveway is shared by the two houses* is possible but reads as a description, not an act).

sign up for.verb type: **action** — dynamic and telic, a single act of enrollment (*forty people signed up for the Saturday session in the first hour*).
sign up for.transitivity: **both** — intransitive with *for* (*I signed up for the two-year plan*), transitive when someone else is enrolled and the particle moves around them: *sign your kids up for swim lessons*, *sign me up*.
sign up for.passive: **restricted** — the causative frame passivizes naturally: *the kids were signed up for swim lessons*. The plain enrollment sense does not: ✗ *the Saturday session was signed up for*.

smile at.verb type: **action** — dynamic, a brief bodily act; the progressive is normal (*she was smiling at the baby*).
smile at.transitivity: **intransitive** — the target always needs a preposition (✗ *smile me*), and the verb stands alone freely (*don't smile*). Only the cognate object survives transitively: *smile a thin smile*.
smile at.passive: **no** for *at* — ✗ *everyone in line was smiled at*, ✗ *the photograph was smiled at*. The one fixed exception is the fortune idiom, where the passive participle is idiomatic: *the weekend was smiled on by the weather*, *a smiled-upon candidate*.

specialize in.verb type: **stative** in practice — it describes what a firm or person characteristically does (*the firm specializes in municipal bond work*), so the progressive is odd except for a change in progress (?*they're specializing in elder law now*).
specialize in.transitivity: **intransitive** — *in* is obligatory: ✗ *specialize immigration law*, ✗ *specialize on bond work*. The verb also stands alone: *you can't specialize in everything*.
specialize in.passive: **no** — intransitive, so there is nothing to promote, and the entry flags the calque directly: ✗ *the firm is specialized in bond work*. American writers use the active, or the noun frame *a specialist in labor law*.

stare at.verb type: **action** — dynamic and durative, an activity you can be caught in the middle of: *two people on the platform were openly staring at her*.
stare at.transitivity: **intransitive** — *at* is obligatory before the target (✗ *stare the screen*), unlike *watch*, which is transitive (*watch the game*). Bare *don't stare* is the absolute use.
stare at.passive: **yes**, restricted to the prepositional passive, which is genuinely idiomatic here — *she was being stared at*, *nobody likes being stared at*. Compare *watch*, which passivizes the ordinary way: *the game was watched by millions*.

stem from.verb type: **stative** — a relation of origin, not an event; it resists the progressive (✗ *the charges are stemming from a 2019 contract*). The homonym *stem the bleeding* is a different, dynamic verb.
stem from.transitivity: **intransitive** — no object in this sense (✗ *stem the problem* belongs to the other verb), and *from* is obligatory: ✗ *the friction stems*.
stem from.passive: **no** — intransitive and stative: ✗ *a 2019 contract is stemmed from*. Only the unrelated homonym passivizes: *the losses were stemmed by the third quarter*.

stipulate to.verb type: **action** — dynamic and performative, a speech act with legal effect the moment counsel makes it (*both sides stipulated to the authenticity of the recordings*).
stipulate to.transitivity: **both** — intransitive with *to* in the agreement sense, transitive in the requirement sense (*the grant stipulates a one-year window*, *stipulate that funds be spent within a year*).
stipulate to.passive: **restricted** — natural in the requirement sense: *it was stipulated that the funds be spent within a year*. The *to* frame passivizes only in legal register and stiffly: ?*the chain of custody was stipulated to*; prefer the active *the parties stipulated to it*.

submit to.verb type: **action** in both senses — dynamic yielding (*he refused to submit to a search*) and dynamic handing-in (*she submitted the form to HR*). Neither is stative, though the yielding sense can describe a standing arrangement: *members submit to the ethics rules when they join*.
submit to.transitivity: **both** — intransitive with *to* in the yielding sense (no object: ✗ *submit a search*), transitive in the filing sense, where the thing submitted is the object and *to* names the recipient.
submit to.passive: **restricted** — the filing sense passivizes constantly and is the standard form: *all bids must be submitted to the purchasing office by Friday*. The yielding sense has no passive: ✗ *a search was submitted to*, ✗ *he was submitted to*.

subscribe to.verb type: **stative** in both senses — holding a subscription and holding a view are states, not acts (✗ *I'm subscribing to that theory*); the inceptive act is *sign up for* or *subscribed* in the simple past.
subscribe to.transitivity: **intransitive** — *to* is obligatory: ✗ *subscribe the print edition*, ✗ *subscribe of that view*. The bare transitive *subscribe an amount* survives only in old securities language.
subscribe to.passive: **no** ordinary passive — ✗ *the print edition is subscribed to by them*, ✗ *three databases are subscribed to*. Only the postmodifying participle survives in formal prose: *a view widely subscribed to among economists*.

substitute for.verb type: **action** — dynamic in both frames: swapping one thing for another (*substitute buttermilk for the whole milk*) and filling in for a person (*she substituted for the regular teacher*).
substitute for.transitivity: **both** — transitive with the **new** item as object and the **old** one under *for*, intransitive in the fill-in sense, where *for* takes the person replaced.
substitute for.passive: **restricted** — the swap frame passivizes: *buttermilk can be substituted for the whole milk*, *a milder resolution was substituted for the one on the floor*. The fill-in sense does not: ✗ *the regular teacher was substituted for*.

succeed in.verb type: **action** — an achievement verb, dynamic and telic; the progressive is limited to the ongoing struggle (*they're succeeding in raising the money*, marked).
succeed in.transitivity: **both** — intransitive in this pattern (✗ *succeed the money*; *in* plus a gerund is the frame, and ✗ *succeed to raise the money* is wrong), transitive in the unrelated sense of following in office: *she succeeded him as chair*.
succeed in.passive: **restricted** — the office sense passivizes normally: *he was succeeded by his deputy*. The *in* frame has no passive: ✗ *raising the money was succeeded in*.

sue for.verb type: **action** — dynamic and telic, the act of filing; *be suing* is normal for a case in progress (*two shareholders are suing for $4 million*).
sue for.transitivity: **both** — transitive with the defendant as object (*she sued the hospital for negligence*), intransitive when only the relief or ground is named (*the contractor sued for the balance*).
sue for.passive: **restricted** — excellent when the defendant is the object: *the hospital was sued for negligence*, *the magazine was sued for running the photograph*. The relief phrase cannot be promoted: ✗ *$4 million is being sued for*.

suffer from.verb type: **stative** in the *from* frame — a condition lived with, though it takes the progressive for temporary ones (*he's suffering from the flu*). The bare transitive is **action**: *he suffered a stroke in March* is a single event.
suffer from.transitivity: **both** — intransitive with *from* naming an ongoing condition or flaw (*the report suffers from relying on a single source*), transitive with a single event and no preposition (*suffer a defeat*, *suffer a loss*).
suffer from.passive: **restricted** — no passive at all for *suffer from*: ✗ *chronic pain is suffered from by one adult in eight*. The transitive object is not a true patient, so its passive is confined to formal financial and military prose: *heavy losses were suffered in the third quarter*, but ✗ *a stroke was suffered by him*.

suspect of.verb type: **stative** — a mental state, not an act; the progressive is marked (?*I'm suspecting the thermostat*), where *investigate* and *accuse* are the dynamic neighbors.
suspect of.transitivity: **transitive** — the person suspected is the direct object and the *of*-phrase names the wrongdoing: *suspected him of moving money*. The object is obligatory: ✗ *investigators suspected of skimming*.
suspect of.passive: **yes** — the exception among stative verbs, and the passive is the commoner form: *she was suspected of leaking the schedule*, *two employees were suspected of falsifying the counts*.

take care of.verb type: **action** — dynamic in both readings, tending (*her neighbor takes care of the plants*) and handling (*I'll take care of the deposit*). Distinguish *take care **to** do*, which is a different frame.
take care of.transitivity: **transitive** as a unit — the whole idiom *take care of* governs the object, and *care* is a frozen noun that takes no article or plural (✗ *take a care of it*).
take care of.passive: **yes** — the prepositional idiom passivizes cleanly, and the entry lists it: *the plants are taken care of while she travels*, *everything except the labor is taken care of by the warranty*.

take precedence over.verb type: **stative** — a relation of rank between two claims that both exist; the progressive is odd (✗ *safety is taking precedence over the schedule*) and so is the imperative.
take precedence over.transitivity: **intransitive** in effect — *precedence* is a frozen noun, not a promotable object (no article, no plural, no modifier beyond *clear* or *absolute*), and the *over*-phrase is droppable when the rival claim is understood: *the more specific provision takes precedence*.
take precedence over.passive: **no** — neither piece can be promoted: ✗ *precedence is taken over the schedule*, ✗ *the schedule is taken precedence over*. Use *supersede* or *override*, which are transitive and passivize: *the state rule is overridden by the federal one*.

talk to, talk with, talk about.verb type: **action** — dynamic and atelic, an activity; the progressive is completely at home (*I'm going to talk with him*, *they were talking about moving*).
talk to, talk with, talk about.transitivity: **intransitive** in all three frames — the preposition is obligatory before a person or a topic (✗ *talk him*, ✗ *talk the budget*). The only transitive uses are fixed: *talk sense*, *talk shop*, *talk business*.
talk to, talk with, talk about.passive: **restricted** — the prepositional passive is idiomatic when a person is affected: *he was talked to about it*, *she's been talked about all spring*. It is weak with topics: ?*moving was talked about*, where *discussed* is the natural transitive substitute.

testify to.verb type: **action** — dynamic and performative, a speech act made under oath; in the figurative use (*the turnout testifies to how much has changed*) it shades **stative**.
testify to.transitivity: **intransitive** — the preposition is obligatory (✗ *testify the authenticity of the ledgers*); for a full proposition the preposition drops and a that-clause follows: *testified that he had seen him leave*.
testify to.passive: **no** ordinary passive — ✗ *the authenticity of the ledgers was testified to by her*. Only the legal postmodifier survives: *the matters testified to by the witness*. Prefer the active or switch to *attest*.

thank for.verb type: **action** — dynamic and performative; *thank you* is the act itself, not a report of one.
thank for.transitivity: **transitive** — the person is a bare direct object and is obligatory (✗ *thank to you*, ✗ *she thanked for coming*); the *for*-phrase naming the favor is optional.
thank for.passive: **yes** — *she was thanked for her service at the last meeting*, *nobody was ever thanked for the extra hours*. Note that *thanks to the ride, I made it* is a different construction entirely and has no active counterpart.

think about, think of.verb type: **both** — **action** when it means deliberate or retrieve (*I've been thinking about it all week*), **stative** when it means hold an opinion (*I think highly of her*, ✗ *I am thinking highly of her*).
think about, think of.transitivity: **both** — intransitive with *about* / *of* plus a noun, gerund, or wh-clause; transitive when the preposition drops before a clause (*think that it's a mistake*) or in the fixed *think it unwise*.
think about, think of.passive: **restricted** — no ordinary passive: ✗ *the offer was thought about by everyone*. But fixed evaluative passives with *of* are fully idiomatic: *she is well thought of in the department*, *it was thought of as a formality*.

touch on.verb type: **action** — dynamic and telic, a brief mention within a longer act of speaking; the second sense (*a politeness touching on contempt*) is **stative** and describes a quality.
touch on.transitivity: **intransitive** — *on* is a fixed preposition, not a movable particle (✗ *touch the subject on*), and it is obligatory: bare transitive *he touched the subject* is a physical act and a different sentence.
touch on.passive: **yes** — the prepositional passive is natural and common in this idiom: *the pension question was touched on only briefly*, *several issues were touched on and none resolved*.

translate into.verb type: **both** — **action** in the language sense (*translated from the Portuguese*), **stative-relational** in the figurative one (*higher volume translates into lower margins*), where the progressive is odd and the claim is a generalization.
translate into.transitivity: **both** — transitive in the language sense (*translate the novel into Spanish*), intransitive in the figurative one (*speed doesn't always translate into wins*) and in the middle voice (*the phrase translates roughly as leave it alone*).
translate into.passive: **restricted** — routine in the language sense: *the novel was translated into eleven languages*, *the report was translated from the Portuguese*. None in the figurative sense: ✗ *lower margins are translated into by higher volume*.

turn on.verb type: **stative** in this pattern — *the case turns on one question* states a dependency, not an act, and the progressive is marked. This is the hinge sense; the switch sense (*turn on the light*) is a dynamic phrasal verb with a movable particle and a different pattern.
turn on.transitivity: **intransitive** — the test is that the object cannot move: *the case turns on one question* but ✗ *turns one question on*, which is exactly what marks *on* as a preposition here rather than a particle.
turn on.passive: **no** in the hinge sense — ✗ *one question is turned on by the case*. The switch sense passivizes freely (*the lights were turned on at six*), and the attack sense too (*he was turned on by the people he trusted*) — three constructions, one spelling.

turn to.verb type: **action** — dynamic and telic, an act of recourse (*he turned to selling insurance*, *she turned to her sister for help*).
turn to.transitivity: **intransitive** — *to* is obligatory (✗ *turn her sister for help*). Watch the purpose infinitive: *he turned to write* is a different sentence in which he swiveled around.
turn to.passive: **no** in ordinary use — ✗ *her sister was turned to for help* is stiff at best; the prepositional passive survives mainly as a postmodifier (*the person most often turned to in a crisis*). Use *consult* or *ask*, which are transitive.

vary with.verb type: **stative-relational** — it asserts covariation, not an event (*demand varies with the weather*); the progressive appears only for observed fluctuation (*the readings are varying*).
vary with.transitivity: **intransitive** in this pattern — no object (✗ *vary the demand with the weather* changes verbs). The separate transitive *vary* means deliberately alter: *vary the routine*.
vary with.passive: **no** — intransitive and stative: ✗ *the weather is varied with by demand*. Only the deliberate transitive passivizes: *the routine was varied to keep them alert*.

vest in.verb type: **action** — dynamic and telic in origin, a legal act of conferring; the resulting *authority is vested in the board* reads as a standing state, which is why the passive dominates.
vest in.transitivity: **transitive** — two frames with the arguments swapped: *vest authority in the board* and *vest the board with authority*. The intransitive *the options vest in four years* is the ordinary time preposition and not this pattern.
vest in.passive: **yes**, and it is the standard form: *authority to approve waivers is vested in the dean's office*, *the power was vested in a single commissioner*. The active is comparatively rare outside statutes.

vote for, vote against.verb type: **action** — dynamic and telic, a single countable act (*every commissioner voted against the rezoning*).
vote for, vote against.transitivity: **intransitive** in this pattern — the preposition is obligatory before a candidate or measure (✗ *vote the levy*), though *vote* also takes a bare to-infinitive (*voted to adjourn*) and a formal that-clause (*voted that the matter be tabled*).
vote for, vote against.passive: **restricted** — ✗ *the bill was voted for by the council* is not idiomatic. The preposition-free particle frames do passivize: *the measure was voted down*, *two incumbents were voted out*. For the prepositional sense use *approve* or *reject*.

vouch for.verb type: **action** — dynamic and performative, putting your own credit behind someone; *I can vouch for that* is the modal use of the same act.
vouch for.transitivity: **intransitive** — *for* is obligatory: ✗ *vouch someone*, ✗ *vouch the accuracy of the transcript*. Compare *guarantee*, which is transitive and takes no preposition.
vouch for.passive: **yes**, restricted to the prepositional passive, which is fully idiomatic here — *he was vouched for by two colleagues*, *every applicant has to be vouched for*.

wait for, wait on.verb type: **action** — dynamic and atelic, an activity that fills time; the progressive is its natural home (*I'm waiting for the inspector*, *she was waiting on tables*).
wait for, wait on.transitivity: **intransitive** — the preposition is obligatory (✗ *wait the bus*), which is what separates it from *await*, transitive and preposition-free: *await further instructions*, ✗ *await for instructions*.
wait for, wait on.passive: **restricted** — the serving sense passivizes naturally: *the customers were waited on promptly*, *you'll be waited on next*. The waiting sense does not: ✗ *the bus was waited for*, ✗ *approval is being waited on*.

warn about, warn against.verb type: **action** — dynamic and performative, a speech act; *about* and *of* describe a danger, *against* prescribes avoiding it.
warn about, warn against.transitivity: **transitive** — the person warned is a bare direct object (✗ *warn to someone*), and the verb also takes a person plus a to-infinitive (*warned her not to sign*) or a that-clause (*warned that the road was flooded*), both preposition-free.
warn about, warn against.passive: **yes** — *residents were warned about the surge*, *she was warned against signing anything*, *drivers were warned that the road was flooded*. The passive is at least as common as the active in news copy.

wish for.verb type: **stative** — a mental state of longing, not an act; the progressive is marked (?*I'm wishing for a raise*) outside seasonal formulas.
wish for.transitivity: **intransitive** with *for* (✗ *wish for going*, ✗ *wish for to go*). Separately **transitive** with a bare infinitive (*wish to speak with the manager*) or a counterfactual past clause (*I wish she were here*), and **ditransitive** in the fixed frames *wish you luck*, *wish him well*.
wish for.passive: **no** — stative and intransitive here: ✗ *a raise was wished for by everyone*. Only the attributive participle survives: *the long wished-for reunion*. The double-object frame does passivize: *they were wished a good trip*.

work on, work for, work with.verb type: **action** — dynamic and atelic in every frame; the progressive is standard (*she's working on the second draft*, *he's been working for the county since 2011*).
work on, work for, work with.transitivity: **intransitive** — each preposition is obligatory (✗ *work the second draft* in this sense, ✗ *work the county*). The unrelated transitives *work the room*, *work the counter*, *work the dough* are a different pattern.
work on, work for, work with.passive: **restricted** — *work on* takes the prepositional passive well: *the second draft is being worked on*, *the roof has been worked on twice*. The others do not: ✗ *the county is worked for by her*, ✗ *the kids are worked with*.

worry about.verb type: **both** — **stative** in *I'm worried about the numbers*, where *worried* is an adjective describing a state; **action** in the habitual *she worries about her mother driving at night*, and in the causative *it worries me*.
worry about.transitivity: **both** — intransitive with *about* plus a noun, gerund, or wh-clause, and with a preposition-free that-clause (*worried that the check would bounce*); transitive when the trouble is the subject: *the estimate worries me*, *don't worry yourself*.
worry about.passive: **yes** for the causative — *I'm worried by how quickly the estimate changed*, closer to *troubled by*. But *be worried about* is an adjectival state, not a passive: it has no active counterpart ✗ *the numbers worry me about*.

answer.verb type: **action** — dynamic and telic (*nobody answered my question*). The *answer to* sense — be accountable — is **stative**: *the inspector general answers to Congress*, a standing reporting line rather than an act.
answer.transitivity: **both** — transitive with no preposition in the reply sense (*answer the question*, *answer the phone*, ✗ *answer to my email*), intransitive when the object is understood (*nobody answered*), and intransitive with *to* / *for* in the accountability senses.
answer.passive: **yes** in the transitive sense — *every email was answered the same day*, *my question was never answered*. No passive of the accountability senses: ✗ *Congress is answered to by the inspector general*.

approach.verb type: **action** — dynamic, and atelic when it means draw near (*the storm approached faster than the forecast allowed for*), which is why the progressive is so common: *enrollment is approaching nine hundred*.
approach.transitivity: **both** — transitive with a bare object (*approach the vehicle*, *approach the problem*, ✗ *approach to the problem*), intransitive with no object at all (*as the deadline approached*). Only *about* attaches: *approached her about the vacancy*.
approach.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the vehicle was approached from opposite sides*, *he was approached about the vacancy and told to put it in writing*. No passive of the intransitive: ✗ *it was approached by winter*.

attend.verb type: **action** — dynamic; the school sense is habitual and reads almost as a state (*he attended three different high schools*), but it still takes the progressive: *she's attending Oberlin*.
attend.transitivity: **both** — transitive with a bare object for presence (*attend the hearing*, ✗ *attend to the meeting* in that sense, ✗ *attend at the conference*), intransitive with *to* for dealing with something (*the nurse attended to him*) and with *on* / *upon* for waiting on someone.
attend.passive: **restricted** — the presence sense passivizes only with a modifier or a by-phrase: *the hearing was attended by about forty people*, *the workshop was well attended*, but bare ✗ *the hearing was attended* is incomplete. *Attend to* has no passive: ✗ *the roof was attended to* is possible but stiff.

contact.verb type: **action** — dynamic and telic, a single completed act of reaching someone (*she contacted three references*).
contact.transitivity: **transitive**, and the object is obligatory: ✗ *I contacted yesterday*, ✗ *I contacted with her*. The whole family behaves this way — *call me*, *email me*, *text me*, *phone the clinic* — and American *write me* joins them, where British English requires *write to me*.
contact.passive: **yes** — *three references were contacted and one wrote back*, *the family has been contacted*. The noun frame supplies the preposition instead: *they've been in contact with the family since Tuesday*.

discuss.verb type: **action** — dynamic and atelic, an activity that occupies time (*we discussed the budget for two hours and settled nothing*).
discuss.transitivity: **transitive**, and the object is obligatory and preposition-free: ✗ *discuss about the budget*, ✗ *discuss on the budget*, ✗ *we discussed for two hours*. The only preposition is *with*, naming the other person, never the topic.
discuss.passive: **yes** — *the budget was discussed for two hours*, *how the shortfall would be covered was never discussed*. The noun keeps its preposition: *a discussion about the merger*.

emphasize.verb type: **action** — dynamic and performative, a speech act (*the memo emphasized the deadline three separate times*).
emphasize.transitivity: **transitive**, object or that-clause obligatory and always preposition-free: ✗ *emphasize on the deadline*, ✗ *emphasize about safety*. *Stress*, *highlight*, *underscore*, and *underline* all behave identically.
emphasize.passive: **yes** — *the deadline was emphasized three separate times*, *it was emphasized that attendance was voluntary*. The preposition belongs to the noun: *heavy emphasis is placed on writing*.

enter.verb type: **action** — dynamic and telic in every sense: crossing a threshold, joining a contest, signing an agreement, keying in data.
enter.transitivity: **both** — transitive and preposition-free in the literal sense (*enter the building*, ✗ *enter into the room*), intransitive in the stage direction (*Enter Hamlet*). *Enter into* is a separate frame for abstractions (*enter into a contract*), and *enter X into Y* for data.
enter.passive: **yes** — *the building was entered through the loading dock*, *the figures were entered into the second field*. The abstraction frame gives a genuine prepositional passive, common in legal prose: *the consent decree was entered into rather than tried*.

lack.verb type: **stative** — the entry says so outright: it names an absence, not an act, and it resists the progressive (✗ *the plan is lacking a mechanism* where *the plan lacks a mechanism* is right). Bare *be lacking* meaning absent is fine: *what's lacking is a budget*.
lack.transitivity: **transitive**, with a bare object that is obligatory and takes no preposition: ✗ *the proposal lacks of detail*, ✗ *the plan lacks in enforcement*. The noun takes *of* (*a lack of detail*) and the participial adjective takes *in* (*lacking in detail*).
lack.passive: **no** — one of the classic stative refusals: ✗ *a mechanism for enforcement is lacked by the plan*, ✗ *confidence has never been lacked by her*. Use *the plan lacks it*, or turn it around: *a second exit is missing*.

marry.verb type: **action** — dynamic and telic, a single event (*she married a man she met in a bus station*). *Be married to* is the resulting state and is adjectival, not a tense of the verb.
marry.transitivity: **both** — transitive with the spouse as a bare object (*marry her*, ✗ *marry with her*, ✗ *marry to him*), transitive with the couple as object when the officiant is the subject (*a justice of the peace married them*), and intransitive (*her sister married young*).
marry.passive: **restricted** — the officiant frame passivizes and is the live passive: *the couple were married by a friend who got ordained online*. The state is not a passive at all: *he's been married to her since 1998* has no active *✗ she marries him*.

oppose.verb type: **both** — mostly **stative**, naming a position held (*every county commissioner opposed the rezoning*), and **action** where it means actively fight something (*they're opposing the permit at every hearing*).
oppose.transitivity: **transitive**, with a bare object or a gerund and no preposition: ✗ *oppose to the merger*, ✗ *oppose against the bill*; *opposed extending the deadline* is correct. The *to* belongs to the adjective *opposed*, which then takes a noun or *-ing*: *opposed to extending the deadline*, ✗ *opposed to extend*.
oppose.passive: **restricted** — the true passive is fine with a by-phrase: *the rezoning was opposed by every county commissioner*. But *the union is opposed to reopening the contract* is the adjective, not a passive — it has no active counterpart ✗ *something opposes the union to reopening*.

protest.verb type: **action** — dynamic and atelic in the demonstrating sense (*students protested the tuition increase for most of the spring*), dynamic and performative in *he protested that nobody had told him*.
protest.transitivity: **both** — transitive with a bare object in American English (*protest the ruling*, where British English requires *protest against the ruling*), intransitive when the crowd simply protests, and with *to* for the official you complain to.
protest.passive: **yes** in the American transitive — *the closure was protested by several hundred people*, *the charge was protested in writing and half of it reversed*. No passive of *protest to*: ✗ *the commissioner was protested to*.

reach.verb type: **action** — an achievement verb, dynamic and telic (*we reached the trailhead about twenty minutes before dark*, *the jury reached a verdict on the second day*).
reach.transitivity: **transitive** with a bare object in the arriving, contacting, and attaining senses: ✗ *reach to the summit*, ✗ *reach at the office*. The prepositional frames are separate verbs of gesture and contact: *reach for the railing*, *reach into a pocket*, *reach out to someone*.
reach.passive: **restricted** — routine with abstract objects and with people: *a verdict was reached on the second day*, *she could not be reached for comment*. Weak with plain destinations: ?*the trailhead was reached before dark* belongs to expedition prose, not ordinary speech.

resemble.verb type: **stative** — the entry says it directly: a relation of likeness, not an act, and it refuses the progressive: ✗ *she is resembling her mother*.
resemble.transitivity: **transitive**, with a bare object that is obligatory: ✗ *resemble to her mother*, ✗ *resemble with her mother*. The noun is where *to* lives: *a striking resemblance to her mother*.
resemble.passive: **no** — the textbook case of a transitive stative that refuses promotion: ✗ *her mother is resembled by her*, ✗ *the rendering was resembled by the building*. The symmetric active is the way around it: *the two dialects resemble each other*.
